messages.subject: New Meeting Format
parts:
With the increased number of participants at each dev meeting
we need to get a little more organized and unless there are
any objections I’m going to change things up on Tuesday.

In order to get important business out of the way before the
meeting becomes too tangential the meeting will now follow a
rigid progression:

1. Roundtable

Everyone very briefly reviews that they’ve been up to in the past
week (less than a minute, maybe more if they have been particularly productive).
This could be removed if there is enough support, but I think it’s
nice to touch base with everyone.

2. Unresolved Topics

These are topics carried over from the past meeting — they won’t
be applicable this week unless there are important issues that
were raised last week. Let me know.

3. New Topics

These are topics of discussion that need to be addressed immediately
or before the next meeting, including questions about modeling or
development, well-posed requests for Stan features, or decisions that
have to be made. New topics not immediately addressed at the meeting
will become “Unresolved topics” to be reviewed the following meeting.

4. Open Discussion Topics

This is what our meetings typically devolve into right now, only hopefully
we can make it a bit more organized. After all proposed discussion
topics have been covered we can open the meeting to other topics.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOU:

If you hate this then let me know and we can try to find a compromise.

If there is anything that you want to have addressed next meeting
add it under “New Topics” at https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Stan-Development-Meeting-Agenda.
If there are any any topics that you would like to discuss add then under
“Open Discussion Topics” at the same place.

This page is not meant for recording minutes or providing an archive
of meeting discussions — it’s just for organizing the meetings week
to week.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: New Meeting Format
parts:
I asked Andrew how GMO was different from MML and didn't
understand the response (we've been going in circles in email
on the same topic --- statisticians and computer scientists
don't speak the same pseudocode).  

I asked Andrew why he wanted GMO when we had ADVI and
I think it came down to his not understanding and/or trusting
ADVI (Andrew's comments are always subtly hedged, so I'm
sure I'm doing him and ADVI a disservice trying to summarize).

1) The two algorithms answer two different questions.

ADVI tries to estimate _all_ marginal _means_.

MML tries to estimate _any_ marginal expectation with
respect to _a few chosen parameters_ (typically hyperparameters
in a hierarchical model).

2) Consequently the two algorithms lives on different points
of the speed/accuracy frontier.  Which is better for a given
application depends on the details of that application, which
means we’re entering into “expert-level knowledge needed”
territory.

Michael has it right. MML only concerns the marginal max of “high-level params” in that equation you write.

To do this, we do gradient descent. Gradient descent requires gradients of the marginal posterior density. This is hard because it’s a gradient of an expectation. Thus there’s an “E-step” in dealing with that expectation.

I think your confusion is about the relationship between EM and MM. You can view EM-type procedures as doing an “MM”, where computing expectations corresponds to maximizing something (for example, variational EM is an approximate “MM”).

Dustin

Remember that everything in statistics (really everything in measure theory)
is expectations. Modes are only useful as a means to approximate
expectations, for example by approximating a target distribution with
a delta function at the mode,

\int dx p(x) f(x) \approx \int dx \delta_{x*} (x) f(x) = f(x*)

where

x* = argmax p(x).

Of course this isn’t parameterization invariant and is an atrocious estimator
in high dimensions unless there is an _insane_ amount of symmetry which
statistically translates to little or no corrections.

MML methods try to take a high dimensional problem and reduce it to a
lower dimensional one. In particular, they partition the parameters x
into two sets, a low dimensional set y and a high dimensional set z,
x = (y, z). If we could marginalize out the y analytically then we could
find the mode of p(y) which might be a useful approximation to some
expectations. In practice we can’t do that, but we can approximate it,
which is what MML methods do.

The key computational step in MML methods is estimating the
conditional p(z | y) and then estimating

p(y) = \int dz p(z | y) p(y).

The conditional and the expectation are typically done with Gaussian
approximations. The importance sampling step in GMO just tries to
correct these approximations to get more accurate estimates of the
marginal density.

messages.subject: GMO and MML
parts:
Hi I don’t know if this will help, but . . .


1.  MML vs GMO

MML is a goal.  GMO is an algorithm.

MML is marginal maximum likelihood (more generally, marginal maximum penalized likelihood).  GMO is gradient-based marginal optimization, an algorithm (or class of algorithms) for reaching the MML solution using a particular approach to computing a simulation-based estimate of the gradient of the marginal likelihood function.  The GMO algorithm is similar to the ADVI algorithm in that it approximates the gradient directly, in contrast to the usual MML algorithms with approximate the marginal lilkelihood and then go from there.  It turns out it can make sense to go for the gradient directly, as we can then make use of the path sampling identity.

MML is to GMO as VB is to ADVI.


2.  Averaging and optimization in GMO

Conditional on the hyperparameters, GMO computes a simulation-based estimate of the gradient of the marginal likelihood.  This is the gradient of an integral, thus an integral of a gradient, thus it’s an integral.  But the way we simulation-estimate this integral is to start with a conditional mode-based approximation.  That’s why I say that GMO has an external optiimzation routine and an internal optimization routine. Really, it has an internal numerical integration routine, but it operates by first performing a conditional optimization.  It would be possible to run GMO without doing an internal optimzation; for example, the internal integral could be estimated using Nuts.  I’ve just been assuming that the mode-based approximation will be faster.

So, the internal integration is a necessary part of GMO.  The internal optimzation is not necessary, but it’s how we’ve been doing things.  The internal optimization is only there as a way to set up the internal integration.

GMO maximizes the marginal likelihood p(y | phi) to get phi^*. As you said, this is the problem of MML; everything else is an extension off that point estimate.

re:covariance. It’s an extension. As Bayesians, we view phi^* as a point mass approximation to the marginal posterior density p(phi | y). A cheap way to get uncertainty is to estimate the covariance of p(phi | y) using the inverse Hessian evaluated at phi^*. We can use this with phi^* to assume a normal approximation to p(phi | y), with mean phi^* and covariance H^{-1}(phi^*). This is like how in lm, it outputs both regression coefficients and their standard errors. Note: this still marginalizes over alpha.

Dustin

There’s a technical snippet that’s worth noting (to Andrew):

If we apply the path sampling identity to take the gradient of the marginal density (not the log marginal density), then there is no longer a ratio of expectations but one expectation. Importance sampling the one expectation gives us a simulation-consistent and also unbiased estimate of that gradient; therefore we can say it performs exact MML. Importance sampling a ratio of expectations as we currently do leads to a biased but simulation-consistent estimate (Appendix E in the write-up has the math). In practice, there’s no reason to do this over the ratio of expectations because optimizing on the original scale is more numerically unstable than optimizing on the log scale. But it’s nice to know that this variant exists.

Dustin

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] GMO and MML
parts:
> And is what people call "empirical Bayes" just
> full Bayes for p(alpha | phi*, y)?

Following Andrew’s point, I don’t know a good name for this. Another phrase thrown around is "Bayesian inference with data-dependent priors”. It is shorthand for "Bayesian inference with priors whose hyperparameters are point-estimated from the data”, which is what Bob wrote above in the case phi are prior hyperparameters. The general notion of “data-dependent priors” is also technically true for full Bayes, since the full posterior p(alpha, phi | y) has “data-dependent priors”. So I don’t know what to call it (if we should even call it something).

> P.S.  Dustin --- I'm putting this in Bayesian terms
> and avoiding max likelihood and std errors on purpose

Cool, we’re on the same page.

Dustin

As to what people call “empirical Bayes,” that’s a flexible term that means different things to different people.  But, yes, it often corresponds to plugging in a point estimate of the hyperparameter.

I’ve been talking about GMO rather than MML because we have typically talked about algorithms.

Thus, GMO, ADVI, NUTS, RMC

On Mar 8, 2016, at 10:29 PM, Andrew Gelman <Gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:


On Mar 8, 2016, at 10:07 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:


On Mar 8, 2016, at 9:49 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

2.  Averaging and optimization in GMO

Conditional on the hyperparameters, GMO computes a simulation-based estimate of the gradient of the marginal likelihood.  This is the gradient of an integral, thus an integral of a gradient, thus it’s an integral.  But the way we simulation-estimate this integral is to start with a conditional mode-based approximation.  That’s why I say that GMO has an external optiimzation routine and an internal optimization routine. Really, it has an internal numerical integration routine, but it operates by first performing a conditional optimization.  It would be possible to run GMO without doing an internal optimzation; for example, the internal integral could be estimated using Nuts.  I’ve just been assuming that the mode-based approximation will be faster.

So, the internal integration is a necessary part of GMO.  The internal optimzation is not necessary, but it’s how we’ve been doing things.  The internal optimization is only there as a way to set up the internal integration.

I also got that part of the algorithm, at least at a high
level, by analogy to ADVI, which Alp wrote in language I
could follow.

But I thought GMO went even further in taking the MML + alpha* thing
point estimate (phi*, alpha*) and created a multivariate normal
approximation of the unconstrained posterior with mean (phi*, alpha*)
and covariance given by the inverse Hessian at (phi*, alpha*).

Then you take a bunch of draws from that multivariate normal and
importance weight them, then transform back to the constrained space.
Now if I take the importance-weighted average of the constrained draws,
I'm not guaranteed to get (phi*, alpha*) as the posterior mean.

So that'd be a rather different algorithm than MML.  But
ADVI really is just an algorithm for computing a particular
variational approximation and otherwise, the solution is the
usual variational approximation.

At each “external” step (that is, guess of phi), GMO approximates the gradient of the integral p(phi,alpha|y) d alpha.  My particular idea of a GMO algorithm (so, I guess we could call this “GMO,” or at least the first recorded flavor of GMO) indeed first computed alpha*, then the normal approximation, then simulations, importance weighting, etc.  Don’t worry about constrained space for now; I’m assuming we’re entirely working in the unconstrained space.  The algoithm as written, with importnace sampling, gives a simulation-consistent estimate of the gradient of the integral.  So it really is a simulation-based approach to getting MML.  In practice, of course we don’t have infinitely many simulation draws so it’s only an approximation to MML, but that’s the same as ADVI and any other simulation-based integration.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] GMO and MML
parts:
With HMC and NUTS I knew the goal was to draw a sample from the posterior.

With GMO the goal is to compute the phi that maximizes p(phi | y) = int p(phi, alpha | y) d alpha.

There are also variants of GMO that compute some approximation. But basic GMO aims for that argmax.

Knowing about lme4 is important if we’re interested in efficiency improvements for GMO. But you don’t need to know about lme4 to understand GMO.
